concepts.name: Nature and Legal Status of SDR
key_dimensions: SDR is NOT a currency nor a claim on the IMF — it is a potential claim on freely usable currencies of IMF members
SDR as an international reserve asset vs. SDR as a unit of account distinction
Why SDR is called a 'basket currency' and the trap: it is not issued by any central bank
SDR vs. currency: SDR cannot be used directly in private transactions

concepts.name: Historical Origin and Evolution of SDR
key_dimensions: Created in 1969 under the Bretton Woods system to supplement gold and US dollar reserves
Context: Triffin Dilemma and the problem of dollar shortage as the trigger for SDR creation
Post-Bretton Woods survival: why SDR remained relevant after the collapse of fixed exchange rates in 1973
Three major allocations: 1970–72, 1979–81, and the landmark 2009 allocation (GFC response) and 2021 allocation (COVID-19)

concepts.name: SDR Basket Composition and Revision Mechanism
key_dimensions: Current basket (post-2016): USD, EUR, CNY, JPY, GBP — the trap being China's RMB inclusion in 2016
Criteria for inclusion: currency of a member with large export share AND 'freely usable' currency designation
Basket reviewed every 5 years by IMF Executive Board — not automatic, requires criteria fulfillment
Weightages in the basket (USD ~41.7%, EUR ~30.9%, CNY ~10.9%, JPY ~8.3%, GBP ~8.1%) and what drives these weights

concepts.name: SDR Valuation and Interest Rate Mechanism
key_dimensions: SDR value calculated daily as a weighted sum of exchange rates of basket currencies against USD
SDR interest rate (SDRi) is a weighted average of short-term government debt instruments of basket currency countries
SDRi is the basis for interest charged on IMF loans AND interest earned on SDR holdings — dual role trap
Who pays interest vs. who earns interest: members holding more than allocation pay interest; those holding less earn it

concepts.name: SDR Allocation Process and Conditions
key_dimensions: Allocations require an 85% supermajority of IMF voting power — making US veto power relevant
General Allocation vs. Special Allocation distinction (Article XV vs. Article XVIII of IMF Articles of Agreement)
2021 allocation of SDR 456 billion (~$650 billion) — largest ever, and the controversy around equitable distribution
Allocations are proportional to IMF quotas — rich countries get more SDRs in absolute terms (a UPSC trap on 'equity')

concepts.name: SDR Holdings, Transactions, and the Voluntary Trading Arrangement
key_dimensions: Members can exchange SDRs for freely usable currencies through voluntary trading arrangements (VTA)
Designation mechanism: IMF can designate members with strong external positions to accept SDRs — compulsory backstop
Who can hold SDRs: IMF members, IMF itself, and 'prescribed holders' (e.g., BIS, ECB, regional development banks) — NOT private entities
India's SDR holdings and transactions with the IMF — relevance to India's foreign exchange reserve reporting

concepts.name: SDR vs. Foreign Exchange Reserves: Accounting and Reporting
key_dimensions: SDR holdings are part of a country's official foreign exchange reserves — reported by RBI in India's case
Distinction between SDR allocation (a liability) and SDR holding (an asset) in a country's balance sheet
India's reserve template: Foreign Currency Assets + Gold + SDRs + Reserve Tranche Position — sequence matters
The trap: SDR allocation increases both assets AND liabilities simultaneously — net position starts at zero

concepts.name: Reserve Tranche Position vs. SDR: Key Differences
key_dimensions: Reserve Tranche = portion of IMF quota paid in foreign currency/SDR, accessible unconditionally — NOT a loan
SDR = separately allocated international reserve asset, not linked to quota payment
Both are part of forex reserves but have different origins, conditionalities, and uses
UPSC trap: both are IMF-related reserve components but Reserve Tranche is country's own money; SDR is allocated

concepts.name: SDR as a Tool for Global Liquidity Management
key_dimensions: SDR allocations inject global liquidity without requiring policy conditionality — key difference from IMF loans
Criticisms: SDRs go to all members including rich ones; poor countries may sell SDRs to rich countries for hard currency
2021 allocation debate: calls for 'rechanneling' SDRs from developed to developing nations through IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)
SDR vs. Quantitative Easing: both expand liquidity but SDR is multilateral and QE is unilateral

concepts.name: Rechanneling of SDRs and the Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)
key_dimensions: G7/G20 commitment to rechannel $100 billion of SDRs to vulnerable countries — voluntary, not mandatory
Mechanisms for rechanneling: through RST, Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT), or direct bilateral loans
RST provides longer-term affordable financing for climate and pandemic resilience — linked to SDR rechanneling
Criticism: rechanneling is slow, voluntary, and converts a 'grant-like' asset into a loan with conditionality

concepts.name: RMB Inclusion in SDR Basket: Geopolitical and Economic Significance
key_dimensions: China's yuan included from October 1, 2016 — first emerging market currency in the basket
IMF's 'freely usable' criterion and debate on whether RMB truly meets it given capital controls
Strategic implications: RMB inclusion accelerates internationalization of yuan and reduces dollar dominance
India's position: INR not in SDR basket — criteria gap (freely usable status) as a policy discussion point

concepts.name: SDR and the Reform of the International Monetary System
key_dimensions: Keynes's 'Bancor' proposal as historical predecessor to SDR concept — reform vision vs. reality
Calls for SDR to replace USD as global reserve currency — Zhou Xiaochuan (PBoC) 2009 proposal
Triffin Dilemma revisited: whether a reformed SDR-based system could resolve the inherent tension
Obstacles to SDR becoming a true reserve currency: no private market, no SDR-denominated bonds at scale

concepts.name: Private SDR (M-SDR) and SDR-Denominated Bonds
key_dimensions: Private SDR (market SDR or M-SDR) concept: using SDR as denomination unit in private financial markets
World Bank issued SDR-denominated bonds (called 'Panda SDR bonds') in China in 2016 — landmark
Limitations: lack of deep liquid markets, no lender of last resort in SDR, currency conversion friction
UPSC angle: difference between official SDR (O-SDR) and market/private SDR (M-SDR)

concepts.name: IMF Quota System and Its Relationship with SDR
key_dimensions: Quota determines: voting power + SDR allocation + access to IMF borrowing — three-in-one link
SDR allocation proportional to quota: countries with larger quotas receive more SDRs absolutely
Quota reform debates (14th and 15th General Review) and implications for SDR distribution equity
India's quota share (~2.75%) and its SDR allocation — specific numbers occasionally tested

concepts.name: SDR Interest Rate (SDRi) and Its Macroeconomic Implications
key_dimensions: SDRi = weighted average of 3-month treasury bill rates of basket currency countries, set weekly
SDRi as floor for IMF concessional lending rates and ceiling for charges on non-concessional lending
Impact of rising US interest rates (e.g., 2022–23 Fed hikes) on SDRi and debt burden of SDR-borrowing countries
SDRi relevance for India: determines cost of India's use of its Reserve Tranche and any SDR-linked borrowings

concepts.name: COVID-19 Pandemic and the 2021 SDR Allocation
key_dimensions: August 23, 2021: SDR 456 billion (~$650 billion) allocation — largest in IMF history, context of COVID recovery
Distribution: ~$275 billion went to advanced economies, ~$212 billion to emerging/developing — equity criticism
India received ~SDR 12.57 billion (~$17.86 billion) — boosted forex reserves significantly
Debate: whether direct budget support vs. SDR allocation is more effective for low-income countries

concepts.name: SDR and India's External Sector Policy
key_dimensions: India's SDR holdings as a component of RBI's forex reserve management and adequacy assessment
India's stance on IMF quota reform and its implications for future SDR allocations
INR internationalization agenda vs. SDR basket inclusion — policy gap and what needs to change
Use of SDR allocation by India: treated as reserve accretion, not deployed directly; macroeconomic impact

concepts.name: Freely Usable Currency Designation and Its Significance
key_dimensions: IMF defines 'freely usable' as: widely used in international transactions AND widely traded in principal exchange markets
Only 5 currencies are freely usable = exactly the SDR basket currencies — NOT a coincidence, this is a definitional overlap
INR is NOT freely usable under IMF definition despite India being a large economy — UPSC trap
Implications: freely usable status affects SDR exchange, quota payments, and IMF loan disbursements

concepts.name: Comparison: SDR vs. Cryptocurrencies as Alternative Reserve Assets
key_dimensions: Both proposed as alternatives to dollar-dominated system, but SDR is state-backed multilateral; crypto is decentralized
IMF's position: crypto cannot fulfill reserve asset functions; SDR has institutional backing and stability
Volatility, scalability, and governance: why SDR has structural advantages despite low usage
UPSC contemporary angle: digital SDR or CBDC-SDR hybrid proposals in G20/IMF discussions

concepts.name: Prescribed Holders of SDR and Institutional Access
key_dimensions: Only IMF members and 'prescribed holders' can hold and transact in SDRs — private entities excluded
Prescribed holders include: BIS, ECB, African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, etc. — NOT World Bank directly
Significance: limits SDR's role as a truly global reserve currency — the 'closed club' problem
UPSC trap: confusing prescribed holders with IMF members; prescribed holders can hold but NOT receive allocations
